text: The checkout test fails about once in eight runs. It clicks the Pay button too early. The slide-in animation is still running. The click lands on the overlay. Playwright reports the button as visible anyway. That is why the failure looks random.

I also set `reducedMotion: 'reduce'` in the test config. The suite then passed 200 runs in a row on CI. I would still keep one retry for now. We should see a full week without failures first.
Paragraph: It now waits for `data-state=open` on the drawer. The drawer sets that attribute after the transition. I also set `reducedMotion: 'reduce'` in the test config. The suite then passed 200 runs in a row on CI. I would still keep one retry for now. We should see a full week without failures first.

The fix is small. I stored the bound handler in a field. I removed it in `destroy()`. Then I added a test.
Paragraph: The fix is small. I stored the bound handler in a field. I removed it in `destroy()`. Then I added a test. It mounts and destroys the panel 500 times. It checks the listener count after each cycle.

It checks the listener count after each cycle. The count now stays at one. Memory on staging stayed flat at 180 MB for two hours. Before the change it climbed past 1.2 GB.
Paragraph: Then I added a test. It mounts and destroys the panel 500 times. It checks the listener count after each cycle. The count now stays at one. Memory on staging stayed flat at 180 MB for two hours. Before the change it climbed past 1.2 GB.

For a local notes app I would pick SQLite. It ships inside the binary. It needs no server process. It keeps the whole database in one file.
Paragraph: For a local notes app I would pick SQLite. It ships inside the binary. It needs no server process. It keeps the whole database in one file. Users can back up that file by copying it. Postgres fits a different case.

Postgres fits a different case. Several clients would write to the same data. That is not the case here.
Paragraph: It keeps the whole database in one file. Users can back up that file by copying it. Postgres fits a different case. Several clients would write to the same data. That is not the case here.

Watch concurrent writes. SQLite allows one writer at a time. WAL mode helps. A single sync worker handles all writes anyway. So the limit should not matter. Later you might add shared workspaces. Then keep SQLite on the client. Put Postgres behind the sync server.

The certificate for `staging.example.dev` expired. Certbot did not renew it. Its timer was disabled. That happened during the OS upgrade in August. Browsers reject the connection. The integration tests reject it too. That explains the red pipeline.
Paragraph: Staging stopped serving HTTPS at 03:12 UTC. The certificate for `staging.example.dev` expired. Certbot did not renew it. Its timer was disabled. That happened during the OS upgrade in August. Browsers reject the connection. The integration tests reject it too. That explains the red pipeline.

The new certificate is valid until January 12. I also added an expiry check to monitoring. It alerts 14 days before a staging certificate runs out.
Paragraph: Then I ran a manual renewal. After that I reloaded nginx. The new certificate is valid until January 12. I also added an expiry check to monitoring. It alerts 14 days before a staging certificate runs out.

The billing export ran twice on Sunday. The cron entry fires at 02:30 local time. Clocks moved back one hour. So 02:30 happened two times. The server runs on `Europe/Berlin`. Cron saw 02:30 before the switch. It saw 02:30 again after it.

Now the schedule runs on UTC. I changed `/etc/cron.d/billing`. I also added a lock file check to `export.sh`.
Paragraph: Now the schedule runs on UTC. I changed `/etc/cron.d/billing`. I also added a lock file check to `export.sh`. It exits early for a date that already finished. The duplicate rows from Sunday are marked.

The duplicate rows from Sunday are marked. I can delete them after finance confirms. Nobody should have used the second file.
Paragraph: I also added a lock file check to `export.sh`. It exits early for a date that already finished. The duplicate rows from Sunday are marked. I can delete them after finance confirms. Nobody should have used the second file.

The migration commit is not gone. Git keeps it in the reflog. The default retention is 90 days. The rebase marked it as `drop`. The todo list was probably edited in a hurry. So `feature/payments` no longer contains it. The object still exists.

Run `git reflog` on the branch. Find the entry from before the rebase. It shows the invoice migration message. Copy its hash. Cherry-pick it onto the current tip. A conflict in `schema.rb` is possible. Keep both column additions. The rebase changed the order of the migrations. It did not change their content.

It reads its config. It exits with code 1 after two seconds. The logs from the previous container show the cause. `DATABASE_URL` is empty. The secret `orders-db` was renamed in release 4.2.0. The deployment still points to the old name.
Paragraph: The `orders-api` pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. It starts. It reads its config. It exits with code 1 after two seconds. The logs from the previous container show the cause. `DATABASE_URL` is empty. The secret `orders-db` was renamed in release 4.2.0. The deployment still points to the old name.

The resolver loads the projects in one query. Then it resolves `owner` for each project. Each call runs its own SELECT. That adds 120 queries per request. The database is fine. The resolver is the problem.
Paragraph: The `projects` query takes 2.8 seconds for a team with 120 projects. The resolver loads the projects in one query. Then it resolves `owner` for each project. Each call runs its own SELECT. That adds 120 queries per request. The database is fine. The resolver is the problem.

I added a DataLoader in `loaders/user.ts`. It batches the owner IDs. It sends one query with an IN clause. It caches the users for the rest of the request.
Paragraph: I added a DataLoader in `loaders/user.ts`. It batches the owner IDs. It sends one query with an IN clause. It caches the users for the rest of the request. The same query now runs in 190 ms. The query count dropped from 121 to 2.

Our webhook endpoint returned 500 for twenty minutes during the deploy. The payment provider retried every failed delivery. It retried without backoff.
Paragraph: Our webhook endpoint returned 500 for twenty minutes during the deploy. The payment provider retried every failed delivery. It retried without backoff. It sent about 35,000 requests in that window. The queue workers fell behind.

The queue workers fell behind. The retries kept arriving. The endpoint kept timing out.
Paragraph: It retried without backoff. It sent about 35,000 requests in that window. The queue workers fell behind. The retries kept arriving. The endpoint kept timing out.

The plan fails with `Error acquiring the state lock`. The lock is real. A CI job took it at 14:05. That job was cancelled. It never released the lock. The DynamoDB table still holds the entry. Its ID is `7f3c9a1e`.

The login fails with `redirect_uri_mismatch`. The app sends `https://app.example.com/auth/callback/`. The provider has `https://app.example.com/auth/callback` registered. The only difference is the trailing slash. Google compares the strings exactly. So the request is rejected. The change came in with router 6.3. It appends slashes to all routes.

On Tuesday the search service was down for 47 minutes. A config change set the connection pool to 5. The previous value was 50. The change passed review. Nobody noticed the missing zero. Traffic peaked at 10:20. The pool ran out.
Paragraph: On Tuesday the search service was down for 47 minutes. A config change set the connection pool to 5. The previous value was 50. The change passed review. Nobody noticed the missing zero. Traffic peaked at 10:20. The pool ran out. Requests queued. Then they timed out.

Der Speicher der Electron-App wächst um etwa 30 MB pro Stunde. Die Ursache liegt in `NotificationBadge.tsx`. Die Komponente registriert einen Listener auf `ipcRenderer`. Sie tut das bei jedem Render. Sie entfernt ihn nie. Nach einem Arbeitstag hängen dort über 2.000 Listener. Jeder hält eine alte Version der Komponente fest.

Jetzt steht die Registrierung in einem `useEffect` mit leerer Abhängigkeitsliste. Die Cleanup-Funktion ruft `removeListener` auf. Danach blieb der Speicher im Test über vier Stunden bei 210 MB.
Paragraph: Jetzt steht die Registrierung in einem `useEffect` mit leerer Abhängigkeitsliste. Die Cleanup-Funktion ruft `removeListener` auf. Danach blieb der Speicher im Test über vier Stunden bei 210 MB. Electron warnt auch nicht mehr vor zu vielen Listenern.
